cases.question: How is an FMLA Eligibility Notice different from a Designation Notice, and when is each generally due?
cases.expected_answer: The Eligibility Notice tells the employee whether they meet eligibility rules and must give a reason if ineligible; it is generally due within five business days of the leave request or learning it may qualify, absent extenuating circumstances. A written Designation Notice tells whether the specific leave counts as FMLA leave, generally within five business days once the employer has enough information, absent extenuating circumstances.
expected_facts: Designation Notice determines whether leave is FMLA-designated
Generally five-business-day timing for each from different triggers
cases.source_hint: Chapters 2 and 6, Eligibility Notice and Designation Notice
cases.actual_answer:
An FMLA Eligibility Notice informs the employee whether they are eligible for FMLA leave and, if not eligible, provides at least one reason for ineligibility. This notice must be provided within five business days of the initial request for leave or upon learning that the leave may be for an FMLA-qualifying reason, unless there are extenuating circumstances. It is given the first time the employee takes leave for an FMLA-qualifying reason in the designated 12-month leave year.

A Designation Notice, on the other hand, informs the employee that the requested leave will be designated as FMLA leave and outlines the requirements applicable while the employee is on leave. This notice must be provided within no more than five business days after the employer has enough information to determine that the leave qualifies as FMLA leave, absent extenuating circumstances. Only one Designation Notice is required for each FMLA-qualifying reason for leave in the 12-month leave year, regardless of whether the leave is continuous, intermittent, or on a reduced schedule.

cases.question: How does NASA distinguish a Concept of Operations (ConOps) from an Operations Concept?
cases.expected_answer: A ConOps is an early, high-level description of how the overall system will be used to meet stakeholder expectations, typically from an operational and time-sequenced perspective; it helps shape requirements and architecture. NASA distinguishes a Concept of Operations (ConOps) as a high-level description developed early in the project that explains how the system will be used to meet stakeholder expectations from an operational perspective, focusing on what is expected without detailing how the design will satisfy those needs. It provides an implementation-free understanding of stakeholder expectations and is typically documented in a ConOps document, model, or Design Reference Mission.

In contrast, an Operations Concept describes how the flight system and ground system work together to ensure the ConOps is reasonable. cases.question: Does Federal OSHA directly cover all state and local government workers? Explain the role of OSHA-approved State Plans.

cases.source_hint: Who Does OSHA Cover / State and Local Government Workers
cases.actual_answer:
Federal OSHA does not directly cover all state and local government workers. Workers at state and local government agencies are not covered by Federal OSHA unless they work in states that have an OSHA-approved State Plan. Every OSHA-approved State Plan must cover state and local government workers.

OSHA-approved State Plans are workplace safety and health programs operated by individual states instead of Federal OSHA. These plans must be at least as effective as the Federal OSHA program and cover state and local government workers. Some State Plans cover both private sector and state/local government workers, while others cover only state and local government workers. In states with State Plans covering only state and local government workers, private sector workers remain under Federal OSHA jurisdiction. OSHA approves and monitors all State Plans and provides up to fifty percent of the funding for each program.
